#1. Compare the distributions of the body heights of the two species from the #'magic_guys.csv' dataset graphically

a. using the basic 'hist' function as well as ‘ggplot’ and ‘geom_histogram’
functions from the ggplot2 package. Optimize the plots for example by trying
several different 'breaks'. Note that ggplot2-based functions give you many
more options for changing the visualization parameters, try some of them.

```{r}
# Inspect the dataset
head(magic_guys)
str(magic_guys)
summary(magic_guys)

# Use ggplot2 to create histogram
library(ggplot2)

hist_guys <- ggplot(magic_guys, aes(x = length, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10,
                 color = "black",
                 alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("jedi" = "blue",
                               "sith" = "red")) +
  labs(title = "Body height distribution: Jedi vs Sith",
       x = "Body height",
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()
```

b. Do the same comparison as in a. but with boxplots. If you want to use the
ggplot2-package, use the functions ‘ggplot’ and ‘geom_boxplot’.

```{r}
box_guys <- ggplot(magic_guys, aes(x = species,
                       y = length,
                       fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5,
               alpha = 0.7,
               outlier.color = "black",
               outlier.shape = 16) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("jedi" = "blue",
                               "sith" = "red")) +
  labs(title = "Body height distribution of Jedi and Sith",
       x = "Species",
       y = "Body height") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

c. Save the plots with the ‘png’, ‘pdf’, and ‘svg’ formats. In which situation would
you use which file format?

```{r}
# Save as "png".
ggsave("Task7_histogram.png",
       plot = hist_guys,
       width = 8,
       height = 6,
       dpi = 300)

# Save as "pdf"
ggsave("Task7_boxplot.pdf",
       plot = box_guys,
       width = 8,
       height = 6)

# Save as "svg"
install.packages("svglite")
library(svglite)
ggsave("Task_boxplot.svg",
       plot = box_guys,
       width = 8,
       height = 6,
       device = "svg")
```
When I need to include the figures for manuscript publication, I would generate "png" or "pdf" or "svg" for high resolution formats, as requsted by journals specifically.


#2. Load the gene expression data matrix from the ‘microarray_data.tab’ dataset
#provided in the shared folder, it is a big tabular separated matrix.

```{r}
microarray_data <- read.delim("microarray_data.tab",
                              header = TRUE)
```

a. How big is the matrix in terms of rows and columns?

```{r}
dim(microarray_data)
nrow(microarray_data)  # Number of rows
ncol(microarray_data)  # Number of columns
```


b. Count the missing values per gene and visualize this result.

```{r}
# Count missing values for each gene
missing_per_gene <- colSums(is.na(microarray_data))

# Display the results
head(missing_per_gene)

missing_data <- data.frame(
  Gene = colnames(microarray_data),
  Missing_values = missing_per_gene
)

ggplot(missing_data, aes(x = Missing_values)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of missing values per gene",
       x = "Number of missing values",
       y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_minimal()
```


c. Find the genes for which there are more than X% (X=10%, 20%, 50%)
missing values.

```{r}
# Calculate percentage of missing values per gene
missing_percentage <- colMeans(is.na(microarray_data)) * 100

# Create a data frame for missing percentage of all genes
missing_percent <- data.frame(
  Gene = colnames(microarray_data),
  Missing_percentage = missing_percentage
)

head(missing_percent)

# 10%
genes_10 <- missing_percent[
  missing_percent$Missing_percentage > 10, ]
genes_10

# 20%
genes_20 <- missing_percent[
  missing_percent$Missing_percentage > 20, ]
genes_20

# 50%
genes_50 <- missing_percent[
  missing_percent$Missing_percentage > 50, ]
genes_50

```


d. Replace the missing values by the average expression value for the particular
gene. (Note: Imputing data has to be used with caution!)

```{r}
gene_means <- colMeans(microarray_data, na.rm = TRUE)
which(is.na(gene_means)) 
sum(is.na(gene_means)) 

# Copy original dataset
microarray_data_clean <- microarray_data

# Replace missing with gene mean
for (i in 1:ncol(microarray_data_clean)) {
  microarray_data_clean[i, is.na(microarray_data_clean[i, ])] <- gene_means[i]
}

# Final check
sum(is.na(microarray_data_clean))

## NOTE!! 34 genes have all missing values, not able to replace

```


#3. Visualize the data in the CO2 dataset in a way that gives you a deeper understanding
#of the data. What do you see?
  
```{r}
data("CO2")

#A.Relationship between CO2 concentration and uptake 
ggplot(CO2, aes(x = conc, y = uptake)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "CO2 uptake versus CO2 concentration",
       x = "CO2 concentration",
       y = "CO2 uptake") +
  theme_minimal()

#B.Effect of treatment on CO2 uptake
ggplot(CO2, aes(x = Treatment,
                y = uptake,
                fill = Treatment)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Effect of treatment on CO2 uptake",
       x = "Treatment",
       y = "CO2 uptake") +
  theme_minimal()

```
